entries.question: Nico controls Analia's [Bane Alley Blackguard] enchanted with their [Corrupted Conscience]. Analia casts their own [Lay Claim], targeting Nico's Corrupted Conscience. After it resolves, who controls the Bane Alley Blackguard? Who controls the Corrupted Conscience?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference: Analia controls both Corrupted Conscience (via Lay Claim) and Bane Alley Blackguard (via Corrupted Conscience's control effect).
entries.answer:
After Lay Claim resolves, Analia controls both the Corrupted Conscience and (as a result) the Bane Alley Blackguard.

Here's why: Lay Claim ("Enchant permanent / You control enchanted permanent") targets and enchants Nico's Corrupted Conscience itself (an Aura is just another permanent, so it's a legal target for Lay Claim's "Enchant permanent"). When Lay Claim resolves, it becomes attached to Corrupted Conscience and, per its own text, Analia now controls the enchanted permanent — Corrupted Conscience. Per rule [303.4e], an Aura's controller is separate from the controller of whatever it's attached to, and changing control of an enchanted object doesn't change control of the Aura enchanting it, and vice versa — so Lay Claim changing control of Corrupted Conscience doesn't by itself move Bane Alley Blackguard, and Corrupted Conscience stays attached to Bane Alley Blackguard without needing to be reattached.

However, Corrupted Conscience's own ability says "You control enchanted creature" (i.e., Bane Alley Blackguard). The "you" in an Aura's textbox refers to whoever currently controls that Aura ([303.4e], [303.4m]). Since Analia now controls Corrupted Conscience, Corrupted Conscience's effect now makes Analia control Bane Alley Blackguard as well. This lines up with the Lay Claim ruling that gaining control of a permanent doesn't automatically hand you control of Auras/Equipment attached to it, or vice versa — control of Bane Alley Blackguard changes here only because Corrupted Conscience's own textual effect is now being applied by its new controller, not because Lay Claim reached through to the creature directly.

End state: Analia controls Corrupted Conscience (via Lay Claim) and Analia controls Bane Alley Blackguard (via Corrupted Conscience, now under Analia's control). Nico ends up controlling neither.

This assumes Lay Claim targeted the Corrupted Conscience Aura itself, as the question states; if it had instead targeted Bane Alley Blackguard, the Lay Claim ruling says gaining control of a creature doesn't transfer control of the Aura attached to it — Nico would keep control of Corrupted Conscience, and there'd be a conflict between Lay Claim's control effect and Corrupted Conscience's control effect resolved by their relative timestamps under rule [701.3c]-style layering, but that's not the scenario asked here.

entries.answer_gold: Analia controls both permanents. Out of the two auras, Corrupted Conscience has the earlier timestamp, and would normally be applied first. However, the effects from both auras apply in the same layer, applying the Lay Claim's effect would change how the Corrupted Conscience's effect is applied, and applying the Corrupted Conscience's effect would not change how the Lay Claim's effect is applied, so the Corrupted Conscience's effect is dependent on the Lay Claim's effect. The Lay Claim's effect applies first, giving Analia control of Corrupted Conscience, and then the Corrupted Conscience's effect applies, giving Analia control of Bane Alley Blackguard.

entries.question: Alan controls [Iroas, God of Victory] and 3 other enchantments. Their devotion to white is 2. They cast [Starfield of Nyx]. After it resolves, is Iroas, God of Victory a creature? If so, what are its power and toughness?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference: Starfield's later type-changing effect makes Iroas a creature and Starfield sets its base power and toughness to its mana value (4/4).
entries.answer:
Yes — after Starfield of Nyx resolves, Iroas, God of Victory is a creature, with base power and toughness 4/4 (not its printed 7/4).

Here's why. Iroas, God of Victory's own text says "As long as your devotion to red and white is less than seven, Iroas isn't a creature." Devotion to red and white is the number of red, white, or red-and-white mana symbols among the mana costs of permanents Alan controls [700.5a][700.5]. With devotion to white at only 2 before casting Starfield of Nyx, and Iroas, God of Victory itself only contributing one {R} and one {W} pip, Alan's devotion to red and white is nowhere close to seven even after Starfield of Nyx (whose cost is {4}{W}) enters and adds one more white pip. So, taken alone, Iroas, God of Victory's own ability would keep it from being a creature.

However, once Starfield of Nyx is on the battlefield, Alan controls five enchantments (Iroas, God of Victory, the three other enchantments, and Starfield of Nyx itself), so Starfield of Nyx's second ability turns on: "each other non-Aura enchantment you control is a creature in addition to its other types and has base power and base toughness each equal to its mana value." Iroas, God of Victory is a non-Aura enchantment Alan controls, so this applies to it.

Both Iroas, God of Victory's "isn't a creature" clause and Starfield of Nyx's "is a creature in addition to its other types" clause are type-changing effects that apply in layer 4 [613.1d]. Continuous effects in a shared layer are applied to the same object in the order determined by when each effect began to apply (and by dependency, if any) [613.6]. Devotion itself is calculated "before any other effects that modify the characteristics of permanents" [700.5a], so Starfield of Nyx's type-changing effect doesn't feed back into the devotion count — there's no dependency between the two effects. That leaves ordinary application order: Iroas, God of Victory's own restriction has been continuously in effect since Iroas, God of Victory entered the battlefield (earlier), while Starfield of Nyx's ability only starts applying once Starfield of Nyx is on the battlefield (later, since it just resolved). Because Starfield of Nyx's "is a creature in addition to its other types" effect is the later one touching the creature-type characteristic, it adds the creature type back on top of whatever Iroas, God of Victory's own ability did, per the "in addition to its other types" rule for retaining/adding types [205.1b]. Net result: Iroas, God of Victory is a creature.

Starfield of Nyx's ability also sets Iroas, God of Victory's base power and toughness equal to its mana value in layer 7b. Iroas, God of Victory's mana cost is {2}{R}{W} (2 generic, 1 red, 1 white), for a mana value of 4, so Iroas, God of Victory becomes a 4/4, overriding its printed 7/4. Its other abilities (indestructible, granting menace, and preventing damage to attacking creatures) are unaffected, since those aren't conditioned on Iroas, God of Victory being a creature.

Assumption on timing: this assumes Iroas, God of Victory was already on the battlefield before Starfield of Nyx entered (as the question states), giving Starfield of Nyx's effect the later timestamp. If instead Iroas, God of Victory somehow re-entered the battlefield after Starfield of Nyx was already established (e.g., it left and came back), Iroas, God of Victory's own "isn't a creature" restriction would then have the later timestamp and would win, making it NOT a creature despite Starfield of Nyx's ability.

entries.question: Nathanael controls [Grizzly Bears] and [Muraganda Petroglyphs]. They cast and resolve [Crowd's Favor], targeting Grizzly Bears. Amia then casts [Archetype of Courage]. After it resolves, what are the power and toughness of Grizzly Bears?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Grizzly Bears is a 5/4 with no first strike, which matches the reference's final ruling.
entries.answer:
Grizzly Bears ends up as a 5/4 with no first strike.

Start: Grizzly Bears is a vanilla 2/2 with no abilities, so Muraganda Petroglyphs' static ability ("Creatures with no abilities get +2/+2") applies to it continuously as long as the condition holds [611.3b]. This is a layer 7c power/toughness‑modifying effect [613.4c], making Grizzly Bears 4/4 before anything else happens.

When Crowd's Favor resolves targeting Grizzly Bears, its effect "Target creature gets +1/+0 and gains first strike until end of turn" is split across layers per rule 613.6: the +1/+0 part is a layer 7c power/toughness effect, and the "gains first strike" part is a layer 6 ability-adding effect. The moment Grizzly Bears gains the first-strike ability, it no longer has "no abilities," so Muraganda Petroglyphs stops applying to it [611.3b] (a permanent that stops meeting the effect's condition loses the effect). At this point Grizzly Bears is a 3/2 (2/2 base +1/+0 from Crowd's Favor) with first strike.

When Amia's Archetype of Courage resolves, its static ability gives "Creatures your opponents control lose first strike and can't have or gain first strike." Grizzly Bears is controlled by Nathanael, who is Amia's opponent, so this layer 6 effect applies to it. Layer 6 effects are applied in timestamp order [613.7], and Archetype of Courage's effect has a later timestamp than Crowd's Favor's grant of first strike, so it applies afterward, stripping first strike from Grizzly Bears and preventing it from having or gaining first strike again (Archetype of Courage's printed text explicitly overrides the general layer/timestamp result that would otherwise let an even-later effect re-grant first strike).

Because layer 6 (abilities) resolves before layer 7 (power/toughness) [613.1g], by the time power and toughness are calculated Grizzly Bears once again has no abilities (first strike having been stripped, and Crowd's Favor's +1/+0 being an effect, not an ability). Muraganda Petroglyphs' "no abilities" condition is therefore satisfied again, and its +2/+2 layer‑7c effect resumes applying to Grizzly Bears.

Final layer 7c math: base 2/2, +2/+2 from Muraganda Petroglyphs, +1/+0 (still active) from Crowd's Favor = 5/4. Grizzly Bears has no first strike (removed by Archetype of Courage) and can't regain it while that effect lasts.

This scenario only involves two players (Nathanael and Amia), so I'm answering for the two-player case; nothing in the provided rules suggests a different outcome in multiplayer, since Archetype of Courage's "creatures your opponents control" wording would apply the same way to any opponent's creatures regardless of table size.

entries.question: Albert controls [Life and Limb], [Blood Moon], and [Murmuring Bosk], that entered the battlefield in that order. Is Murmuring Bosk a creature?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the opposite conclusion—saying Bosk is a creature under timestamp ordering—while the reference says Blood Moon prevents Life and Limb from making it a creature.
entries.answer:
Yes — under a timestamp-order application of the layer 4 type-changing effects, Murmuring Bosk ends up as a land creature (a Land Creature — Mountain Saproling, 1/1 green), still under the effects of both Life and Limb and Blood Moon.

Here's the reasoning, assuming the order given (Life and Limb entered first, then Blood Moon, then Murmuring Bosk):

1. Murmuring Bosk's printed type line is Land — Forest [Murmuring Bosk]. Per its own ruling, "Murmuring Bosk is a Forest, but it isn't a basic land" [Murmuring Bosk ruling #0] — i.e., it has the basic land type Forest but lacks the supertype "basic" [205.4c].

2. Type-changing effects (like both Life and Limb's and Blood Moon's) are layer 4 effects, applied in timestamp order [613.1d]. Life and Limb entered the battlefield before Blood Moon, so it has the earlier timestamp and is applied first in that layer.

3. Life and Limb reads: "All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types" [Life and Limb]. Since Murmuring Bosk has the Forest subtype at the point this effect is applied, it becomes a 1/1 green Saproling creature that is also still a land, retaining its other types [Life and Limb ruling #3, 205.3c, 305.6].

4. Blood Moon's effect, "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" [Blood Moon], is applied next (later timestamp). Murmuring Bosk is a nonbasic land [Murmuring Bosk ruling #0], so this effect sets its land subtype to Mountain, replacing Forest. Critically, rule 305.7 states that "Setting a land's subtype doesn't add or remove any card types (such as creature) or supertypes ... the land may have." So this does not strip away the creature card type or the Saproling creature subtype Life and Limb already granted — it only swaps the land type from Forest to Mountain.

So the end result, applying the effects strictly in timestamp order, is that Murmuring Bosk is a Land Creature — Mountain Saproling, 1/1 and green, and Blood Moon's own text ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") overrides what land type it has, while Life and Limb's text is what makes/keeps it a creature.

A caveat on timing: this answer assumes the two static effects are simply ordered by timestamp per rule 613.1d, which is the only layer-application rule provided here. Magic's full rules also include a "dependency" provision for cases where one effect's applicability is altered by whether another effect has already been applied — and here, Life and Limb only affects things that are Forests, while Blood Moon is exactly the kind of effect that could remove that Forest status. That dependency rule isn't among the rules given to me, so I can't confirm from the provided material whether it would force Blood Moon to be evaluated before Life and Limb (which could instead mean Murmuring Bosk is not a creature, since Blood Moon would have already turned it into a plain Mountain before Life and Limb's "all Forests" ability checked it). Based purely on the timestamp-order rule I do have (613.1d), the creature outcome above is correct, but be aware a fuller dependency rule could change it.

entries.answer:
Cinder Glade ends up as a plain nonbasic Mountain with no Forest type and only a single mana ability, while the 1/1 green Saproling Creature token becomes a land creature (a Forest in addition to being a Saproling) that Blood Moon does NOT touch.

Why: Blood Moon's effect ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") and Life and Limb's effect ("All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types") are both type-changing effects that apply in layer 4 [613.6]. When two layer-4 effects both try to affect the same object's types, they're applied in timestamp order (the order the abilities came into existence), and Blood Moon's ability has been around longer than Life and Limb's, since Blood Moon entered the battlefield first.

Cinder Glade: Cinder Glade (Land — Mountain Forest) has no "basic" supertype, so it's a nonbasic land even though its land types happen to be basic land types [205.4c, Nonbasic Land]. Blood Moon's layer-4 effect is applied to it first (earlier timestamp): per [305.7] and [Blood Moon ruling #2], setting a land's subtype to a basic land type strips its old land types and the abilities generated by its rules text (so it loses "Mountain Forest," the "tap: add R or G" ability, and the "enters tapped unless..." ability) and it gains only the land type Mountain and the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {R}." Because Blood Moon's effect is applied before Life and Limb's within layer 4, by the time Life and Limb checks "all Forests," Cinder Glade is no longer a Forest — it's just a Mountain — so Life and Limb has nothing to grab onto here. Result: Cinder Glade is simply a nonbasic land, type Mountain, with the sole ability "{T}: Add {R}." It is not a creature.

The Saproling token: A token only has the characteristics its creating effect defined [111.3], so before any of this the token is just a 1/1 green Saproling creature — not a land, and thus not something Blood Moon's "nonbasic lands" clause can touch at all. When layer 4 is applied, Blood Moon's (earlier-timestamp) effect is checked against the board first; at that point the Saproling token still isn't a land, so Blood Moon skips it. Then Life and Limb's effect applies: since the token has the creature type Saproling, Life and Limb makes it "a 1/1 green Saproling creature and Forest land in addition to its other types" [Life and Limb ruling #1, Life and Limb ruling #3]. It keeps its creature type (Saproling) and card type (creature), and now also gains the card type land and the land subtype Forest, per [205.1b] ("in addition to its other types" preserves everything it already had) and [205.3c] (Saproling stays correlated to creature, Forest stays correlated to land). Because it only becomes a land after Blood Moon's pass through layer 4 has already happened, Blood Moon never gets a chance to turn it into a Mountain. As a Forest, it gains the intrinsic mana ability "{T}: Add {G}" [305.6]. Result: the token is now a 1/1 green Land Creature — Forest Saproling, with "{T}: Add {G}," and it is unaffected by Blood Moon.

(Timing note: this assumes the customary rule that same-layer effects without dependency are ordered by timestamp of the affecting permanents, which is how [613.6]'s framework is applied here alongside the specific rulings on these two cards. All four permanents' relative entry order given in the question — Blood Moon, then Life and Limb, then Cinder Glade, then the Saproling — is exactly what fixes this timestamp order.)

Applying Life and Limb's effect first would allow Blood Moon's effect to apply to the Saproling, and applying Blood Moon's effect first would prevent Life and Limb from applying to the Cinder Glade, so both effects are dependent on each other and those dependencies are ignored. Spend this mana only to cast an instant or sorcery spell." and its Craft ability), and it is a creature subject to summoning sickness. With that ability gone, there is no effect making Furycalm Snarl or Crosis's Catacombs into Mountains, so they keep exactly their own printed land types, subtypes, and mana abilities. Important caveat: this exact scenario is a classic "does an ability-removal effect undo a type-changing effect that the removed ability already generated" puzzle. Determining the truly rules-correct outcome requires the full continuous-effects layer system (the specific order of layers, e.g., type-changing vs. ability-removing) and the dependency rule that resolves effects that reference each other's results. Rule [613.1] only gives the general framework (characteristics are built up through a series of layers) but the actual enumerated layer order and the dependency provisions aren't included in the rules I have available, so I can't confirm from the given rules whether a fixed layer order would let the type-change "lock in" before Humility strips the ability. entries.question: Aiden controls [Volrath's Shapeshifter] and [Yixlid Jailer]. The top card of their graveyard is [Mistform Skyreaver]. Does Volrath's Shapeshifter have flying?
entries.reason: Both conclude Volrath's Shapeshifter gains Mistform Skyreaver's printed text (including Flying) and Yixlid Jailer only strips abilities from the card in the graveyard, so the Shapeshifter still has flying.
entries.answer:
Yes. With Mistform Skyreaver on top of Aiden's graveyard, Volrath's Shapeshifter has Flying (and Mistform Skyreaver's activated ability), in addition to its own granted "{2}: Discard a card" ability.

Volrath's Shapeshifter's ability reads, "As long as the top card of your graveyard is a creature card, this creature has the full text of that card..." Per rule [612.6], having the "full text" of another object changes Volrath's Shapeshifter's name, mana cost, color indicator, power, toughness, and rules text to match Mistform Skyreaver's printed text -- meaning Volrath's Shapeshifter becomes (in effect) a 6/6 blue Illusion named Mistform Skyreaver with Flying and "{1}: This creature becomes the creature type of your choice until end of turn," plus it keeps the granted "{2}: Discard a card" text as stated on its own card and confirmed by [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #1] ("this card keeps the granted ability in addition to those from the card being copied").

Yixlid Jailer's static ability, "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities," is an ability-removing effect [113.10] that strips Flying and the activated ability directly off Mistform Skyreaver while that card sits in the graveyard. Crucially, rule [612.3] states that effects which add or remove abilities don't change the *text* of the objects they affect -- an ability-removing effect like Yixlid Jailer's doesn't rewrite Mistform Skyreaver's printed text, it only strips the ability off that particular object. Since Volrath's Shapeshifter's ability grants it the *full text* of the top graveyard card (not a copy of its current, ability-stripped state), it still picks up Flying and the mana-type-changing ability from Mistform Skyreaver's text.

Separately, even setting that aside: Yixlid Jailer's effect only applies to "cards in graveyards." Once Volrath's Shapeshifter (a permanent on the battlefield) has acquired that text, it is not itself a card in a graveyard, so Yixlid Jailer's ability-stripping effect has no ongoing effect on Volrath's Shapeshifter's acquired abilities.

This analysis assumes Mistform Skyreaver is currently on top of the graveyard and stays there without another card being placed on top in the interim; if a non-creature card were later put on top, Volrath's Shapeshifter would revert to being just a 0/1 blue creature with only its own "{2}: Discard a card" ability, per [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #0].

entries.answer_gold: Yes. Yixlid Jailer only removes abilities, not text, and text is what Volrath's Shapeshifter cares about. Volrath's Shapeshifter also gains the text of the Mistform Skyreaver before Yixlid Jailer removes the abilities.

entries.question: Aspen controls [Watchwolf] enchanted by [Lignify], [Figure of Destiny] that's had its third ability activated, and [Swab Goblin]. They casts [Pack's Favor] targeting Swab Goblin. After that resolves, they casts [Mirrorweave] targeting Figure of Destiny. What are the characteristics of Swab Goblin and Watchwolf?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference: Watchwolf is a 0/4 Treefolk with no abilities (Lignify overwriting the copy) and Swab Goblin is a copy of Figure of Destiny with base 1/1 plus Figure's activated abilities and is currently 4/4 due to Pack's Favor.
entries.answer:
Watchwolf ends up as a 0/4 red‑and‑white creature named "Figure of Destiny" with the type Treefolk and no abilities (still wearing the Lignify Aura). Swab Goblin ends up as a red‑and‑white creature named "Figure of Destiny" with the type Kithkin, base power/toughness 1/1 (currently 4/4 thanks to the still‑active Pack's Favor pump), and it now has Figure of Destiny's three activated abilities.

Here's why. Mirrorweave says "Each other creature becomes a copy of target nonlegendary creature until end of turn," and it targets Figure of Destiny, so both Watchwolf and Swab Goblin (everything Aspen controls other than Figure of Destiny itself) become copies of it. A copy only acquires the *copiable values* of the thing it's copying — name, mana cost, color (derived from mana cost), types, rules text, and printed power/toughness — not any P/T or type changes produced by that object's own non-"enters the battlefield" abilities [707.2a]. Figure of Destiny's activated abilities ("{R/W}: becomes a Kithkin Spirit 2/2," etc.) are ordinary activated abilities, not "as…enters" abilities, so its current 8/8 flying first‑strike Kithkin Spirit Warrior Avatar state (from having activated its third ability) is *not* copied — this is exactly the Chimeric Staff situation described in the rules: a Clone copying a Chimeric Staff that had become a 5/5 creature ends up as the plain artifact, not the 5/5, though it still has the Staff's ability [707.2]. So both Watchwolf and Swab Goblin copy Figure of Destiny's printed characteristics: name "Figure of Destiny," mana cost {R/W}, colors red and white, type Creature — Kithkin, base power/toughness 1/1, and the three activated abilities as printed text [707.1] [707.2] [613.2a].

For Watchwolf, Lignify is still attached (Mirrorweave doesn't remove Auras) and its text — "Enchanted creature is a Treefolk with base power and toughness 0/4 and loses all abilities" — is a separate, ongoing (noncopy) effect. Becoming a copy "doesn't change any noncopy effects presently affecting the permanent" [707.4], so Lignify keeps overwriting: the copied Kithkin subtype is replaced by Treefolk, the copied base 1/1 is overwritten to base 0/4, and the three copied activated abilities are stripped away by "loses all abilities" — the same way Lignify's ruling confirms it overwrites characteristic‑defining abilities for power/toughness and creature type [Lignify ruling #5]. Color isn't mentioned by Lignify, so Watchwolf keeps the red/white color it got from Figure of Destiny's {R/W} mana cost.

For Swab Goblin, there's no Aura or other overriding effect, so it simply becomes the copy described above (name Figure of Destiny, Kithkin, base 1/1, red/white, with the three activated abilities). However, Pack's Favor's "+3/+3 until end of turn" is also a noncopy effect that was already affecting Swab Goblin, and per the same rule it isn't removed by the later copy effect [707.4]; it keeps applying on top of the new base 1/1, making Swab Goblin currently a 4/4 until end of turn (though its base power/toughness is 1/1).

This scenario is unambiguous about ordering since the question states Pack's Favor fully resolved before Mirrorweave was cast, so no alternate-timing caveat is needed here.

entries.question: Allison controls [Dralnu's Crusade] and [Leopard-Spotted Jiao]. Allison then casts [Conspiracy] naming "Goblin". What are the creature types of Leopard-Spotted Jiao and does it get +1/+1?

entries.question: Aya controls a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters on it. Nico casts [Duplicant] and has it exile Skullbriar, the Walking Grave. What are Duplicant's power and toughness after the imprint ability resolves?

Duplicant ends up 4/4. Skullbriar, the Walking Grave has printed power/toughness 1/1, and it has 3 +1/+1 counters on it. Skullbriar's own text says "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library," and since Skullbriar has that ability while it's still on the battlefield (the zone it's moving from), the 3 +1/+1 counters travel with it into exile. Per rule 122.1a, a +1/+1 counter "on a creature or on a creature card in a zone other than the battlefield" still adds to that card's power and toughness, so while sitting in exile Skullbriar, the Walking Grave is a 4/4 creature card (1/1 base plus 3 +1/+1 counters).

Per Duplicant's own rulings, Duplicant's power and toughness are constantly updated to match the exiled card's actual current power and toughness (Duplicant ruling #3), not just its printed values -- the only thing that's carved out is that abilities which merely add or subtract power/toughness (like Death's Shadow's) don't apply while the card sits in exile (Duplicant ruling #2). Counters aren't an 'ability that adds or subtracts' in that sense; they are markers that directly modify the object's characteristics under rule 122.1a in any zone, so they're part of what Duplicant copies. Since Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's counters remain on it in exile and make it 4/4 there, Duplicant takes on those same power and toughness values: Duplicant becomes a 4/4 (still a Shapeshifter, per its own text) as long as Skullbriar, the Walking Grave stays exiled with the counters on it.

This assumes the 3 +1/+1 counters were already on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave before Duplicant's imprint ability exiled it, and that nothing (like Yixlid Jailer-type effects) strips Skullbriar's own counter-retention ability before it leaves the battlefield; if such an effect were in play, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave would lose its counters on the way to exile and Duplicant would instead become a 1/1.

This is applied in layer 7b, at which point Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's power and toughness is still 1/1 because power and toughness changes from counters are not applied until layer 7c.

Layer 7: Sublayer 7b applies effects that set base power/toughness (rule 613.4b; see also the "Base Power, Base Toughness" definitions and rule 208.4a/208.4b). Sublayer 7c applies power/toughness-modifying effects, such as the threshold ability's "+3/+3." Crucially, rule 613.6 states that once an effect starts applying across multiple layers, it keeps applying in each applicable layer "even if the ability generating it is removed during this process." Wayward Angel's threshold ability is a single continuous effect whose components land in layers 5, 6, and 7c; even though its layer-6 component (granting trample/the sac ability) got wiped out by Turn to Frog's later-timestamped ability removal, its layer-7c component (+3/+3) still applies, because the threshold condition (7+ cards in the graveyard) is still true and the effect had already begun applying. entries.question: Addison controls [Dryad of the Ilysian Grove] and casts [Blood Moon]. What are the characteristics of [Snow-Covered Island], [Study Hall], [Dryad Arbor], and [Mountain] after Blood Moon resolves?
entries.reason: The candidate gives the same final characteristics as the reference: basic lands keep their "basic" supertype and gain all five basic subtypes from Dryad, while nonbasic lands (Study Hall and Dryad Arbor) are set to Mountains by Blood Moon (Dryad Arbor remaining a creature land).
entries.answer:
After Blood Moon resolves: Snow-Covered Island and Mountain (both basic lands) are untouched by Blood Moon and instead only reflect Dryad of the Ilysian Grove's effect, while Study Hall and Dryad Arbor (both nonbasic lands) get overwritten by Blood Moon down to plain Mountains.

- Snow-Covered Island: Blood Moon only affects "nonbasic lands," and Snow-Covered Island is a basic land (it has the supertype "basic" per [205.4c]), so Blood Moon does nothing to it. Dryad of the Ilysian Grove's static ability ("Lands you control are every basic land type in addition to their other types") still applies, so Snow-Covered Island is now a Basic Snow Land — Plains Island Swamp Mountain Forest, keeping its "basic" and "snow" supertypes ([205.4b]) and gaining the intrinsic mana ability of each basic type per [305.6]: {T}: Add {W}, {T}: Add {U}, {T}: Add {B}, {T}: Add {R}, and {T}: Add {G} [Dryad of the Ilysian Grove ruling #0].

- Mountain (the basic land card): Same reasoning — it's a basic land, so Blood Moon ignores it. Dryad of the Ilysian Grove adds all five basic land types to it "in addition to" its existing type, so it becomes Basic Land — Plains Island Swamp Mountain Forest with all five basic mana abilities ({T}: Add {W}/{U}/{B}/{R}/{G}), still a basic land named "Mountain."

- Study Hall: Study Hall has no basic-land supertype, so it counts as "nonbasic" for Blood Moon even after Dryad of the Ilysian Grove would otherwise add basic land types to it. Per [Blood Moon ruling #2], "Nonbasic lands will lose any other land types and abilities they had. They will gain the land type Mountain and gain the ability '{T}: Add {R}.'" This matches rule [305.7]: setting a land's subtype to a basic land type strips its old land types and any abilities generated by its rules text, and grants only the new type's mana ability. So Study Hall becomes a nonbasic Land — Mountain with only "{T}: Add {R}"; it loses its printed "{T}: Add {C}" ability and its commander-mana/scry ability, and it does not end up with the other four basic types Dryad of the Ilysian Grove would otherwise grant. It is still named Study Hall and is still not a basic land (Blood Moon doesn't add the "basic" supertype, per [Blood Moon ruling #1] and [305.7]).

- Dryad Arbor: Dryad Arbor is also nonbasic, so Blood Moon likewise sets it to Mountain and strips its old land type (Forest) and the mana ability that came with it. However, Dryad Arbor's card type (Land Creature) and creature type (Dryad) are not land subtypes, so they're untouched — per [Dryad Arbor ruling #0] and [Dryad Arbor ruling #2], "If Dryad Arbor is changed into another basic land type, it continues to be a green Dryad creature," and its green color comes from its color indicator, which applies in all zones regardless of type changes ([Dryad Arbor ruling #3]). [205.1b] and [205.4b] confirm that changing subtypes doesn't strip card types or supertypes. So Dryad Arbor becomes a nonbasic Land Creature — Mountain Dryad, still green, still 1/1, now with "{T}: Add {R}" instead of "{T}: Add {G}", and it still isn't a spell and still counts as your land play for the turn ([Dryad Arbor ruling #4]). It does not gain the other four basic types from Dryad of the Ilysian Grove, per the same Blood Moon overwrite described above.

Note: none of this changes any land's name, and none of the nonbasic lands become basic lands — Blood Moon only sets the land type, never the "basic" supertype ([Blood Moon ruling #1], [305.7], [205.4c]).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Snow-Covered Island and Mountain have all basic land subtypes: "Plains", "Island", "Swamp", "Mountain", and "Forest". Dryad of the Ilysian Grove doesn't change supertypes and Blood Moon affects nonbasic lands.

Study Hall has subtype Mountain. There are no dependencies between Dryad of the Ilysian Grove and Blood Moon, so we apply the type-changing effects in timestamp order.

Dryad Arbor is now a Creature Land - Dryad Mountain. Gaining a basic land type doesn't remove other card types or nonland subtypes.

entries.question: Nico controls [Thespian's Stage] that's currently a copy of [Temple of Triumph]. Alayna casts [Alpine Moon] and names "Temple of Triumph" as it resolves. Alayna then activates a second Thespian's Stage targeting Temple of Triumph. What does each Thespian's Stage look like?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Alayna's Thespian's Stage remains a full Temple of Triumph with its mana ability, whereas the reference says both stages end up only with "{T}: Add one mana of any color" (no other abilities).
entries.answer:
Short version: after all this, Nico's original Thespian's Stage becomes a name-only husk that just taps for one mana of any color, while Alayna's second Thespian's Stage becomes a full, working copy of Temple of Triumph (tapping for {R} or {W}) that keeps Thespian's Stage's own copy-activation ability.

Walking through it:

1) Nico's first Thespian's Stage is already "a copy of Temple of Triumph." Per Thespian's Stage's own text ("…becomes a copy of target land, except it has this ability"), its copiable values are those of Temple of Triumph plus its own retained activation ability [707.9b, 707.9c]. Its name, per those copied values, is now literally "Temple of Triumph."

2) When Alayna's Alpine Moon resolves naming "Temple of Triumph," its ability reads: "Lands your opponents control with the chosen name lose all land types and abilities, and they gain '{T}: Add one mana of any color.'" Alpine Moon does not touch supertypes or other card types, only land types and abilities [Alpine Moon ruling #1]. This is a dynamic, name-based continuous effect that checks the object's current name, so it doesn't matter that the Thespian's Stage got that name by copying rather than being printed with it. Since Nico's Thespian's Stage is now named "Temple of Triumph" and is controlled by Alayna's opponent (Nico), it is caught by Alpine Moon: it loses all its abilities — the copied "enters tapped," the copied scry-1 trigger, the copied "{T}: Add {R} or {W}," and even its own retained "{2},{T}: become a copy of target land" ability, since Alpine Moon strips *all* abilities with no exception — and it gains "{T}: Add one mana of any color" instead. It keeps the name "Temple of Triumph" (Alpine Moon doesn't rename anything) but is now functionally just a plain any-color land.

3) Alayna then activates her second Thespian's Stage (I'm assuming she controls this one, since she's the one activating it — the puzzle doesn't say otherwise, and only a permanent's controller can normally activate its abilities) targeting the actual Temple of Triumph permanent. A copying permanent's copiable values are the target's printed values as modified only by *other copy effects*, not by other continuous effects like Alpine Moon's ability-stripping [707.3; Thespian's Stage ruling #3]. So Alayna's Thespian's Stage copies Temple of Triumph's real printed text: name "Temple of Triumph," enters tapped, an ETB scry-1 trigger, and "{T}: Add {R} or {W}" — plus it keeps its own "{2},{T}: This land becomes a copy of target land, except it has this ability" per its own wording [707.9b]. Because Thespian's Stage was already on the battlefield, the "enters tapped" and scry-1 triggers do not fire, and it does not untap just because Temple of Triumph is untapped [Thespian's Stage ruling #1, ruling #2]. Now, even though this land is also named "Temple of Triumph," Alpine Moon only affects lands *Alayna's opponents* control — since Alayna controls this Thespian's Stage herself, Alpine Moon does not touch it. So it remains a fully functional copy of Temple of Triumph with its mana ability intact and its own copy-ability intact.

Note on timing/order: I'm assuming Alpine Moon fully resolves (and its naming choice is locked in) before the second Thespian's Stage activation, as the question's sequence states. If instead the second Thespian's Stage activation happened before Alpine Moon resolved, the analysis of what it copies wouldn't change (it still copies Temple of Triumph's printed values), but Alpine Moon's ability-stripping would still apply afterward to whichever of Nico's lands ends up named "Temple of Triumph" at that time.

Multiplayer note: this scenario is framed as two players. If there were more than two players at the table, Alpine Moon's "lands your opponents control" would apply to *every* opponent of Alayna's who controls a land named "Temple of Triumph," not just Nico's — the underlying logic above wouldn't change, just the number of affected permanents.

Also worth flagging: if it turns out Nico (not Alayna) actually controls the second Thespian's Stage, then that Stage's post-copy name ("Temple of Triumph") would make it controlled by Alayna's opponent too, and Alpine Moon would strip its abilities down to just "{T}: Add one mana of any color" exactly like the first Stage.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Both Thespian's Stages are lands named "Temple of Triumph" and have "{T}: Add one mana of any color." and no other abilities. Because Thespian's Stage gains its ability as part of the copying process, the ability applies in the copy layer, which is earlier than the adding and removing abilities layer.

entries.question: Allen controls [Thraben Purebloods] which is enchanted by [Kenrith's Transformation]. Thraben Purebloods then becomes enchanted by [One with the Stars]. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate left Kenrith's Transformation attached/uncertain and claimed both Auras remain, while the reference states Kenrith becomes illegal and is put into the graveyard, yielding a different final state.
entries.answer:
Because One with the Stars was attached after Kenrith's Transformation, its type-setting effect has the later timestamp and wins in layer 4: Thraben Purebloods ends up as just an enchantment, no longer a creature at all.

Here's why, working through the layers (rule 613.7 says effects in the same layer apply in timestamp order, and rule 613.9 confirms that when two effects don't depend on each other, the later-timestamped one simply wins for whatever it changes):

- Layer 4 (card type): Kenrith's Transformation's text says Thraben Purebloods 'is a green Elk creature...(It loses all other card types and creature types.)' Because its Aura attached first, this applies first, turning Thraben Purebloods into a plain Elk creature (per Kenrith's Transformation ruling #3, it overwrites all prior types/creature types, keeping only supertypes, and there are none here). One with the Stars then attaches later and its text says 'Enchanted permanent is an enchantment and loses all other card types' (One with the Stars ruling #2: it also strips subtypes tied to the lost card types, so the 'Elk' subtype goes too). Since this is a later timestamp acting on the same layer 4 type-setting, it overrides the previous result: Thraben Purebloods is now simply an enchantment, not a creature and not an Elk.
- Layer 5 (color): Kenrith's Transformation's 'is a green...' clause still applies untouched (One with the Stars doesn't touch color), so the permanent remains green.
- Layer 6 (abilities): Kenrith's Transformation's 'loses all abilities' clause still applies, so it has no abilities (One with the Stars doesn't grant any).
- Layer 7b (power/toughness): Kenrith's Transformation's 'base power and toughness 3/3' still technically applies as a characteristic, but since Thraben Purebloods is no longer a creature, power and toughness have no functional relevance.

So the end state is: a green enchantment named Thraben Purebloods, with no abilities, still wearing both Auras, but it is not a creature.

One important wrinkle I can't fully confirm from the rules given here: Kenrith's Transformation's own printed text is 'Enchant creature.' Once Thraben Purebloods stops being a creature, Kenrith's Transformation would seemingly be attached to an object it isn't allowed to enchant. Ordinarily that kind of illegal-attachment situation is handled by a state-based action that sends the Aura to its owner's graveyard, but the specific state-based-action rule for an Aura attached to something it can no longer legally enchant was not included in the rules provided to me, so I can't verify from what's given here whether Kenrith's Transformation gets put into the graveyard as a result. If you want that confirmed, the relevant rule would need to be checked separately.

entries.answer_gold:
Thraben Purebloods becomes an enchantment with no abilities and with the color dictated by Kenrith's Transformation. When state-based actions are checked, Kenrith's Transformation is attached to an illegal target and is put into the graveyard. Thraben Purebloods then regains all characteristics except its type is only enchantment. State-based actions are checked again. Nothing happens, and Allen gets priority.

This is an interaction of continuous effects, so the layers will need to be considered. In this case, no changes occur until layer four. There are two effects occurring in this layer, so timestamps will need to be considered. Since Kenrith's Transformation was attached first, Thraben Purebloods maintains its status as a creature. Then, One with the Stars turns Thraben Purebloods into an enchantment and removes all other types. Thraben Purebloods is changed to the color dictated by Kenrith's Transformation in layer five. Thraben Purebloods loses all abilities in layer six due to Kenrith's Transformation. Lastly, Thraben Purebloods has its power and toughness set to the values stated in Kenrith's Transformation in layer seven. When state-based actions are checked, Kenrith's Transformation is attached to an enchantment and is put into the graveyard. State-based actions are checked again, and nothing happens.

entries.question: Avery manifests the top card of their library with [Soul Summons]. Then, they mutate [Trumpeting Gnarr] targeting the manifested creature. What are the characteristics of the resulting creature if Avery chooses to put the manifested creature on top?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly says the merged permanent keeps Trumpeting Gnarr's triggered ability and it triggers, but the correct ruling is the topmost face-down component makes the merged permanent a 2/2 colorless face-down creature with no abilities, so Gnarr's ability does not apply or trigger.
entries.answer:
When Avery chooses to keep the manifested card on top, Trumpeting Gnarr's mutating creature spell goes underneath it, and the resulting merged permanent is face down: a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, no creature types, and no mana cost, but it also has the triggered ability "Whenever this creature mutates, create a 3/3 green Beast creature token" from Trumpeting Gnarr.

Here's why. As the mutating creature spell (Trumpeting Gnarr cast for its mutate cost) resolves and its target (the manifested creature) is still legal, it doesn't enter the battlefield on its own; instead it merges with the manifested creature to become one merged permanent [702.140c][608.3d]. Avery, as the mutate spell's controller, chooses whether Trumpeting Gnarr goes on top or on the bottom of the manifested creature; in this case Avery puts the manifested card on top, so Trumpeting Gnarr ends up underneath it [702.140c].

Rule 702.140e says a mutated permanent has *all* abilities of every card/token that represents it, but its *other* characteristics (name, types, mana cost, power/toughness, etc.) come only from the topmost card or token. Since the manifested card is on top, and Soul Summons's manifest ability put it onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2 creature, the topmost component's characteristics are those of a face-down permanent: a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, no card types beyond 'creature', no subtypes, and no mana cost (Soul Summons's reminder text: 'Put it onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2 creature'). This also makes the whole merged permanent's status face down, per rule 730.2e, which states that when a merged permanent has both face-up and face-down components, its status is determined by its topmost component — here that's the still-hidden manifested card.

However, the abilities clause of 702.140e is not limited to the topmost card, so the merged permanent also has Trumpeting Gnarr's printed ability 'Whenever this creature mutates, create a 3/3 green Beast creature token,' even though Trumpeting Gnarr itself is now the bottom, face-down-irrelevant component. In fact, that ability actually triggers off this very mutate event as the merge happens, producing a separate 3/3 green Beast token, but that token is a distinct permanent, not part of the merged creature's characteristics.

Note: this assumes Avery's manifested card hasn't already been turned face up before the mutate spell resolved; if it had instead already been turned face up into a creature card before mutating, the topmost component's characteristics used in 702.140e would instead be that face-up card's actual printed characteristics rather than the generic 2/2 vanilla face-down stats.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It is a 2/2 colorless face-down creature with no abilities. It is face-down because the topmost object is face-down, and this status defines its characteristics. This notably means that Trumpeting Gnarr's triggered ability won't trigger.

entries.question: April casts [Spontaneous Flight] targeting their [Mist Dragon]. After that resolves April then activates its 'lose flying' ability. They cast another Spontaneous Flight targeting Mist Dragon. After that resolves they then use [Hex Parasite] to remove one flying counter. Does Mist Dragon have flying?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Mist Dragon does not have flying because it treats the grant-from-counter effect as having a fixed timestamp that isn't refreshed by adding another counter, which contradicts the reference ruling that the second counter updates the timestamp so the remaining counter out-timestamps the lose-flying effect (so the reference says yes).
entries.answer:
No — after all these events, Mist Dragon does not have flying. Here is the timeline of the continuous effects affecting flying on Mist Dragon, tracked by timestamp order (the method used in [613.7a] and illustrated in [613.9]):

1. First Spontaneous Flight resolves (t1): it puts a flying counter on Mist Dragon (count 0→1). This creates the continuous effect "Mist Dragon has flying" that exists because it has a flying counter; by [613.7a], that effect's timestamp is the timestamp of the effect that created the ability — i.e., t1, when the count first became nonzero. At this point Mist Dragon has flying.

2. April activates Mist Dragon's own '{0}: This creature loses flying' ability. It resolves (t2, later than t1), creating an indefinite continuous effect "Mist Dragon loses flying." Neither the grant-from-counter effect nor this remove effect depends on the other, so per [613.9] they're applied in timestamp order: grant (t1) then remove (t2). The later effect wins, and Mist Dragon loses flying (per [113.10b], an effect that removes an ability removes all instances of it that exist at that point).

3. Second Spontaneous Flight resolves (t3): it puts a second flying counter on Mist Dragon (count 1→2). Because Mist Dragon already had at least one flying counter (the count never dropped to zero), this does not create a brand-new instance of the "has flying" ability with a fresh, later timestamp — the ability granted by having a flying counter was already created at t1 and simply continues to exist ([613.7a]: the effect's timestamp is fixed at when it was created, not refreshed by reinforcing the same already-true condition). So the grant effect's timestamp stays at t1, still earlier than the t2 removal effect. Applying grant(t1) then remove(t2) again, Mist Dragon still lacks flying immediately after the second Spontaneous Flight resolves (it does, however, get another +2/+2 until end of turn from that spell).

4. Hex Parasite then removes one flying counter (count 2→1). Mist Dragon still has one flying counter remaining, so the counter-based grant effect is still present, still timestamped t1 (it never dropped to zero, so nothing resets). Nothing about the timestamp ordering changes: t1 (grant) is still applied before t2 (remove), so the removal continues to be the effect that determines the final state. Mist Dragon still does not have flying.

Note also [702.9c]: multiple instances of flying on the same creature are redundant anyway, so the two flying counters were never 'stacking' the ability — having a second counter while the first was already present doesn't add anything extra, consistent with it not generating a new later-timestamped grant.

Assumption/caveat: the key interpretive step is treating the ability granted by 'having a flying counter' as a single ongoing ability whose creation-timestamp is fixed the first time the counter count became nonzero, per the literal wording of [613.7a] ('the timestamp of the effect that created the ability'). If instead every individual counter placement were treated as generating its own fresh timestamped instance of the ability, the second Spontaneous Flight's counter (t3, after the loses-flying activation at t2) would have restored flying, and removing one of the two counters afterward could then go either way depending on which counter's instance survived. Based on the general timestamp rule as given, I'm treating it as not refreshing, so the answer is that Mist Dragon does not have flying.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Keyword counters and ability-removing effects all apply in layer 6 in timestamp order. However when April put the second flying counter on Mist Dragon all flying counters on Mist Dragon had their timestamps updated to match the most recent counter. Meaning that the remaining flying counter on Mist Dragon has a newer timestamp than the activation of the ability that causes it to lose flying.

entries.question: Aimee controls [Fiend Artisan] and has four creature cards in their graveyard. Nico enchants it with [Mystic Subdual]. What is the power and toughness of Fiend Artisan?
entries.reason: Both conclude Mystic Subdual removes Fiend Artisan’s +1/+1 ability in layer 6 and then applies -2/-0 to its 1/1 base in layer 7, yielding a -1/1.
entries.answer:
Fiend Artisan ends up as a -1/1 creature. Fiend Artisan is printed 1/1, and its static ability ("This creature gets +1/+1 for each creature card in your graveyard") is a power/toughness-modifying ability that applies in layer 7c [613.4c] — it is not a characteristic-defining ability that sets base power/toughness, as confirmed by [Fiend Artisan ruling #2], which notes the ability only functions while Fiend Artisan is on the battlefield (i.e., it's an ordinary static ability, not a rule-604.3 CDA). Mystic Subdual's enchanted-creature effect gives two separate continuous effects that apply in different layers per [613.6]: "loses all abilities" applies in the abilities layer (layer 6), and "-2/-0" applies in the power/toughness layer, sublayer 7c [613.4c]. Because ability removal happens in an earlier layer than the power/toughness sublayers, Fiend Artisan's own +1/+1-per-graveyard-creature ability is stripped away before layer 7 is evaluated, so it contributes nothing regardless of how many creature cards (four, in this case) are in Aimee's graveyard. What's left is Fiend Artisan's base 1/1 [302.4c], modified only by Mystic Subdual's -2/-0 in layer 7c: 1-2 power = -1, 1-0 toughness = 1. This mirrors the logic in [Mystic Subdual ruling #1] for */*-style creatures whose defining ability is stripped, though Fiend Artisan's case is simpler since its base printed power/toughness (1/1) never depended on a characteristic-defining ability in the first place — only its bonus did, and that bonus's ability was removed by Mystic Subdual's 'loses all abilities' clause, which as printed card text overrides the general expectation that Fiend Artisan would otherwise be a 5/5 (1/1 base + 4/4 from four graveyard creatures). This is a two-player-neutral interaction; nothing about graveyard counting or Mystic Subdual's text changes in a multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Fiend Artisan is a -1/1. In layer 6 Mystic Subdual eliminates the abilities of Fiend Artisan. In layer 7 Mystic Subdual gives Fiend Artisan -2/-0, making it a -1/1. Its ability to gain +1/+1 from each creature card in Aimee's graveyard does not apply, as it was removed.

entries.question: Nico controls [Humility]. Avalyn controls [Maritime Guard] and wants to cast [Glowstone Recluse] mutating onto the Maritime Guard and putting it on top. What will the resulting creature's P/T be?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the mutated creature will be a 1/1 with no abilities and that Humility prevents the Glowstone Recluse mutate trigger from ever firing.
entries.answer:
The merged creature ends up as a 1/1 with no abilities — the two +1/+1 counters from Glowstone Recluse's mutate trigger never get put on it. Here's why: When Glowstone Recluse mutates onto Maritime Guard and is placed on top, the resulting permanent's other characteristics (including base power/toughness) are derived from the topmost card, Glowstone Recluse, and it has all abilities of both Glowstone Recluse and Maritime Guard [702.140e]. The merge itself establishes these as the object's starting characteristics — base power/toughness 2/3 from Glowstone Recluse, applied in layer 1a as a copiable/merge-defined value [613.2a] — and this is the starting point before any continuous effects from other permanents are layered on [613.1]. Humility, which Nico controls, is a continuous effect that says 'All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1.' The ability-removal portion applies in layer 6, and it strips every ability off every creature, including the mutated Glowstone Recluse/Maritime Guard permanent — this means the 'Whenever this creature mutates, put two +1/+1 counters on it' ability granted by Glowstone Recluse is removed by Humility's continuous, ongoing effect. Because Humility has been continuously affecting the battlefield since before this creature came into being, the merged creature never actually has that ability at the moment mutation occurs [702.140d], so the trigger never fires and no +1/+1 counters are ever put on it. Separately, Humility's power/toughness-setting effect applies in layer 7b [613.4b], setting base power and toughness to 1/1, which overwrites the 2/3 base established from the merge in layer 1a (layer 7b is applied after layer 1a, so Humility's 1/1 is the final value). Card text on Humility ('lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1') overrides what the general mutate rules would otherwise grant, per the printed-text-wins principle. Net result: the merged permanent (Glowstone Recluse mutated onto Maritime Guard) is a 1/1 vanilla creature — no Reach, no mutate trigger, no counters — as long as Humility remains on the battlefield. This assumes no other timestamped effects intervene; if some other effect later removes Humility, the mutate ability would return and the base P/T would revert to 2/3 (the mutate trigger itself already having failed to fire is not retroactively fixed).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 1/1 with no abilities, since mutate impacts the creature in layer 1 and Humility acts in layers 6 and 7. It will also not trigger Glowstone Recluse because Humility applies constantly and it's never on the battlefield without being affected.

entries.question: Alex controls [Magus of the Moon] and [Forgotten Monument]. Neil casts [Lizard, Connors's Curse] targeting Magus of the Moon. After Lizard, Connors's Curse has resolved, what are the characteristics of Forgotten Monument?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling: Forgotten Monument remains a Mountain land that taps for {R} because Magus of the Moon's subtype-changing effect has already applied and continues to apply even after Magus loses its abilities.
entries.answer:
Forgotten Monument remains a Mountain — its characteristics don't change at all as a result of Lizard, Connors's Curse resolving. Before Lizard, Connors's Curse even entered the battlefield, Magus of the Moon's static ability "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" had already turned Forgotten Monument (a nonbasic land) into a Mountain: per Magus of the Moon ruling #4, it loses its old land type (Cave) and its printed abilities (both "{T}: Add {C}" and "Other Caves you control have '{T}, Pay 1 life: Add one mana of any color'"), gains the land type Mountain, and gains the mana ability "{T}: Add {R}" (rule 305.7). It keeps any supertypes it had (Magus of the Moon ruling #1; it isn't legendary here anyway) and it is not renamed "Mountain" (Magus of the Moon ruling #1).

Now, Lizard, Connors's Curse's Lizard Formula ability triggers when it enters and targets Magus of the Moon (a legal target, since it's a creature), causing Magus of the Moon to lose all its abilities and become a 4/4 green Lizard creature with no other abilities. You might expect this to shut off the "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" effect and let Forgotten Monument revert to being a Cave with its original text. However, Magus of the Moon ruling #0 states directly: "If Magus of the Moon loses its abilities, it continues to turn nonbasic lands into Mountains. This is because effects that change subtypes are applied before considering effects that remove abilities, regardless of the order in which those effects started." This reflects the general continuous-effects rule that once a layer/sublayer effect has started applying to a set of objects, it keeps applying to those objects even if the ability generating it is later removed (rule 613.6).

So after Lizard, Connors's Curse resolves and its enters-the-battlefield ability also resolves (stripping Magus of the Moon's abilities), Forgotten Monument is unaffected and remains: a nonbasic land with the land type Mountain (having lost the Cave type and its own printed rules text), whose only ability is the intrinsic "{T}: Add {R}" that comes from being a Mountain (rule 305.6). It is colorless (lands have no color absent a special effect) and has mana value 0.
